newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK money growth eases, Bank warns on RPI.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK money growth eases, Bank warns on RPI.

text.p: British broad money supply growth slowed in April but the Bank of England renewed its warning that interest rates might have to rise again soon to stop inflation getting out of hand.

The central bank said on Wednesday M4 money supply, which is often seen as a pointer to future inflationary pressures, rose 0.3 percent in April from the previous month, giving an annual growth rate of 10.4 percent.
This was down on the March annual figure of 11.2 percent but was still well outside the three to nine percent monitoring range set by the last Conservative government.

Although the figures were better than financial markets had expected, Bank of England Governor Eddie George said his job was to take "pre-emptive action" to prevent robust economic growth reaching unsustainable levels.
"At the moment, in the short run, it's extremely encouraging. There are very, very few inflationary pressures to be seen anywhere in the system," he told BBC radio.

But he added: "What we're also seeing is robust domestic demand growth at a rate which can't be sustained for very long without actually that giving rise to inflationary pressures further down the track."
The Bank of England was given responsibility for setting interest rates earlier this month in a radical move by new Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown.

Brown raised interest rates to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent only days after the May 1 election, in his first and last such decision as finance minister. The Bank has since made clear that it believes further rate rises will be needed.

City economists said the slowdown in M4 money supply growth might take some pressure off the Bank to go for an early rate increase, but it would be premature to conclude that the trend of robust growth had been reversed.

Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets, said the April figures had been flattered by a surprise surplus in government finances and activity on the gilt repo market, in which British government bonds are used as security for short-term borrowing.

"In any case, as long as it remains in double figures, the Bank will continue to argue that the growth of M4 is inconsistent with the (2.5 percent) inflation target and hence maintain the pressure for tighter policy," he said.
In the Bank of England annual report, published on Wednesday, George said that while the strong pound was helping to dampen inflationary pressures, its effects were likely to ease in time.
The effect of the pound on trading sectors of the economy could not be ignored.

"But nor can we expose the whole of the rest of the economy to significant inflationary risks which would then need to be addressed by a more abrupt tightening of policy at a later stage," George said.
